subject: maths
title: Angles at a point and vertically opposite angles
summary: Using the rules for angles on a straight line (180°), angles at a point (360°), complementary angles (90°) and vertically opposite angles to find missing angles.
body:
When straight lines cross or meet, the angles they make follow simple rules. Builders use these rules to check that walls and roof beams line up, and designers use them to split a circle into equal slices — like a pizza or a pie chart. In this lesson you will use three angle rules to find missing angles without a protractor.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can find unknown angles using the rules for angles on a straight line, angles at a point, complementary angles and vertically opposite angles, and give a reason for each step.

## Before you start

You need Measuring and classifying angles (Year 7), especially that a straight angle is 180° and a full turn is 360°. You also need to add and subtract whole numbers quickly.

**Warm-up**

1. Work out 180 − 74.
2. Work out 360 − (100 + 150).

*Answers:* 1. 106 2. 110

## Think of it like this

### Sharing out a pizza

A whole pizza is a full turn — 360°. However you cut it, the slices around the centre always add back up to the whole pizza. Cut a pizza in half with a straight cut and each half is 180° — so any slices on one side of that cut must add to 180°.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* pizza slices are usually cut into equal pieces, but the angles in a diagram can all be different sizes — only their total is fixed.

## Key ideas

### Angles on a straight line add to 180°

If two or more angles sit side by side on a straight line, sharing a vertex, they add to 180°. These are called **angles on a straight line**. Two angles that add to 180° are called **supplementary angles**.

Example: if one angle on a line is 62°, the angle next to it is 180° − 62° = 118°.

![A straight line with a ray from a point on it, making angles of 62° and 118° that sit side by side](/diagrams/y7/maths/angles-at-a-point-and-vertically-opposite-angles-line.svg)

### Angles in a right angle add to 90°

If angles fill a right angle, they add to 90°. Two angles that add to 90° are called **complementary angles**.

### Angles at a point add to 360°

Angles that go all the way around a point, with no gaps or overlaps, make a full turn. **Angles at a point** add to 360°.

### Vertically opposite angles are equal

When two straight lines cross, they make four angles, an X shape. The angles **opposite** each other across the crossing point are called **vertically opposite angles**, and they are always **equal**.

Why? Picture lines crossing with angles a, b, c, d going round. a and b sit on a straight line, so a + b = 180°. b and c also sit on a straight line, so b + c = 180°. Both a and c are "180° take away b", so a = c.

![Two straight lines crossing, making four angles a, b, c and d going round the crossing point; a is opposite c and b is opposite d](/diagrams/y7/maths/angles-at-a-point-and-vertically-opposite-angles-abcd.svg)

("Vertically" here means "at the vertex" — it has nothing to do with up and down.)

### Use letters for unknowns and give reasons

Diagrams often label an unknown angle with a letter, like a° or x°. When you find it, write the rule you used as your reason, for example "angles on a straight line add to 180°" or "vertically opposite angles are equal". Teachers give marks for the reason as well as the number.

### Angles written with algebra

Sometimes angles are written as expressions like 2x or x + 20. You add them up and use the rule to make an equation. For example, if x and 2x are on a straight line, then x + 2x = 180, so 3x = 180 and x = 60.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 47°. Find the other angle, a°.

![A straight line with a ray making an angle of 47° and, next to it on the line, the unknown angle a](/diagrams/y7/maths/angles-at-a-point-and-vertically-opposite-angles-ex1.svg)

Step 1: Angles on a straight line add to 180° — this is the rule to use.
Step 2: a = 180 − 47 — subtract the angle you know.
Step 3: a = 133.
Check: 133 + 47 = 180 ✓

### Example 2

A right angle is split into two angles. One is 34°. Find the other angle, b°.

![A right angle split by a ray into an angle of 34° and the unknown angle b](/diagrams/y7/maths/angles-at-a-point-and-vertically-opposite-angles-ex2.svg)

Step 1: The angles fill a right angle, so they add to 90° — they are complementary.
Step 2: b = 90 − 34 = 56.
Check: 56 + 34 = 90 ✓

### Example 3

Four angles meet at a point: 140°, 95°, 70° and c°. Find c.

![Four angles around a point: 140°, 95°, 70° and the unknown angle c](/diagrams/y7/maths/angles-at-a-point-and-vertically-opposite-angles-ex3.svg)

Step 1: Angles at a point add to 360° — they make a full turn.
Step 2: Add the angles you know: 140 + 95 + 70 = 305.
Step 3: c = 360 − 305 = 55.
Check: 140 + 95 + 70 + 55 = 360 ✓

### Example 4

Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles is 62°. Find the other three.

![Two straight lines crossing; one angle is 62° and the other three angles are marked with question marks](/diagrams/y7/maths/angles-at-a-point-and-vertically-opposite-angles-ex4.svg)

Step 1: The angle vertically opposite 62° is also 62° — vertically opposite angles are equal.
Step 2: The angle next to 62° is on a straight line with it, so it is 180 − 62 = 118°.
Step 3: The angle opposite that one is also 118° — vertically opposite angles are equal.
Check: 62 + 118 + 62 + 118 = 360 ✓ (angles at a point)

### Example 5

Three angles at a point are x°, 2x° and 3x°. Find x.

Step 1: Angles at a point add to 360°, so x + 2x + 3x = 360.
Step 2: Collect like terms: 6x = 360.
Step 3: Divide both sides by 6 — to get x on its own: x = 60.
Check: 60 + 120 + 180 = 360 ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Using 360° for a straight line (or 180° for a point).** This happens when you rush. Fix: ask "Is it half a turn (a line) or a full turn (all the way round)?"
- **Thinking angles next to each other are equal.** Neighbouring angles at a crossing add to 180°; only the *opposite* ones are equal. Fix: equal = across the X.
- **Leaving out an angle when adding.** It is easy to miss one in a busy diagram. Fix: tick each angle as you add it.
- **Mixing up complementary and supplementary.** Fix: use the tip below.
- **Giving the number with no reason.** Fix: write the rule in words next to each answer.

## Tips to remember

- **C comes before S, and 90 comes before 180:** **C**omplementary = 90°, **S**upplementary = 180°. A common trick: "**C** for **C**orner (a right-angle corner), **S** for **S**traight."
- **Straight line = half a pizza = 180°. Whole point = whole pizza = 360°.**
- **The X rule:** in an X, the angles that face each other like a mirror are twins. (Made-up memory trick.)
- **Quick self-check:** at any crossing, the four angles must add to 360°, and you should only see two different sizes.

## Key terms

- **Angles on a straight line** — angles side by side on a line that add to 180°.
- **Supplementary angles** — two angles that add to 180°.
- **Complementary angles** — two angles that add to 90°.
- **Angles at a point** — angles around one point that add to 360°.
- **Vertically opposite angles** — the opposite angles made when two lines cross; they are equal.

## Summary

- Angles on a straight line add to 180° (supplementary).
- Angles that make a right angle add to 90° (complementary).
- Angles at a point add to 360°.
- When two lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal; neighbouring ones add to 180°.
- Always write the rule as your reason.
- If angles are written with algebra, add them, set equal to 180 or 360, and solve.

questions.prompt: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One is 73°. What is the other?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so 180° − 73° = 107°. 287° comes from using 360°, which is for angles at a point.
steps: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

mistakes.B: Step 1: angles on a straight line add to 180°, not 90°.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a straight line is half a turn (180°), not a full turn (360°).
mistakes.D: Step 1: neighbouring angles on a line add to 180° — they are not equal.

questions.diagram_alt: A straight line with a ray making an angle of 73° and, next to it, an unknown angle marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One of the angles is 58°. What is the angle vertically opposite it?
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the opposite angle is also 58°. 122° is the neighbouring angle on the straight line, not the opposite one.
steps: The angle across the crossing point is vertically opposite.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 180° − 58° = 122° is the angle NEXT to 58°, not the one opposite it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: vertically opposite angles are equal; you subtracted from 90°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: vertically opposite angles are equal; you subtracted from 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Two straight lines crossing; one angle is 58° and the angle opposite it across the crossing point is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Two angles are complementary. One is 28°. What is the other?
questions.explanation: Complementary angles add to 90°, so 90° − 28° = 62°. 152° is what you get if you mix it up with supplementary (180°).

mistakes.A: Step 1: complementary angles add to 90°; 180° is for supplementary angles.
mistakes.B: Step 1: complementary angles add to 90°, not 360°.
mistakes.C: Step 1: complementary angles add to 90° — they don't have to be equal.

questions.prompt: Three angles meet at a point: 120°, 150° and a°. Find a.
questions.explanation: Angles at a point add to 360°: 120 + 150 = 270, and 360 − 270 = 90. 30 comes from using 300 instead of 360, or 270 comes from forgetting to subtract.
steps: Angles at a point add to 360°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 270 is the total of the known angles — subtract it from 360.
mistakes.D: Step 1: angles at a point add to 360°, not 330° — check your total.

questions.diagram_alt: Three angles around a point: 120°, 150° and the unknown angle a

questions.prompt: Three angles sit side by side on a straight line: 48°, 65° and b°. Find b.
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add to 180°: 48 + 65 = 113, and 180 − 113 = 67. 247 comes from using 360°.
steps: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 1: angles on a straight line add to 180°, not 360°.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 113 is the total of the known angles — subtract it from 180.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 48 + 65 = 113, not 103 — remember to carry the ten.

questions.diagram_alt: Three angles side by side on a straight line: 48°, 65° and the unknown angle b

questions.prompt: Four angles meet at a point: 110°, 85°, 90° and c°. Find c.
questions.explanation: Angles at a point add to 360°: 110 + 85 + 90 = 285, and 360 − 285 = 75. 285 is the total of the known angles, not the missing one — you still need to subtract it from 360.
steps: Angles at a point add to 360°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you left out the 90°. Add all three known angles: 110 + 85 + 90.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 285 is the total of the known angles — subtract it from 360.

questions.diagram_alt: Four angles around a point: 110°, 85°, a right angle (90°) and the unknown angle c

questions.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 38°. What are the other three angles?
questions.explanation: The opposite angle equals 38°, and each neighbouring angle is 180° − 38° = 142°. 52° comes from subtracting from 90° instead of 180°.
steps: The angle vertically opposite 38° is also 38°.
The neighbouring angles are on a straight line with 38°, so each is 180° − 38° = 142°.
So the other three are 38°, 142° and 142° (check: 38 + 142 + 38 + 142 = 360 ✓).

mistakes.B: Step 2: neighbouring angles add to 180°, not 90°.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the angle opposite 38° is equal to it (38°), not 142°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: neighbouring angles add to 180° (a straight line), not 360°.

questions.prompt: Three angles on a straight line are x°, x° and (x + 30)°. Find x.
questions.explanation: The angles add to 180°: 3x + 30 = 180, so 3x = 150 and x = 50. 60 comes from ignoring the + 30 and doing 180 ÷ 3.
steps: Angles on a straight line add to 180°: x + x + x + 30 = 180.

mistakes.A: Step 2: don't forget the + 30 — the angles are 3x + 30, not 3x.
mistakes.C: Step 3: subtract 30 from both sides (150), don't add it (210).
mistakes.D: Step 1: angles on a straight line add to 180°, not 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Three angles side by side on a straight line, marked x°, x° and (x + 30)°

questions.prompt: Angles at a point are in the ratio 4 : 5. The larger one is a reflex angle. How big is it?
questions.explanation: 4 + 5 = 9 parts make 360°, so one part is 40° and the larger angle is 5 × 40° = 200°. 100° comes from sharing 180° instead of 360°.
steps: The two angles are at a point, so they add to 360°.
There are 4 + 5 = 9 parts, so one part is 360° ÷ 9 = 40°.

mistakes.A: Step 1: angles at a point add to 360°, not 180°.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 4 × 40° = 160° is the smaller angle; the larger one is 5 parts.

questions.prompt: Two straight lines cross. Two vertically opposite angles are (2x + 10)° and (3x − 20)°. What is the size of each of the other two angles?
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal: 2x + 10 = 3x − 20 gives x = 30, so these angles are 70°. The other two angles are 180° − 70° = 110°. 70° is the size of the first pair, not the ones asked for.
steps: Subtract 2x from both sides: 10 = x − 20, then add 20: x = 30.
So each of these angles is 2 × 30 + 10 = 70°.
The other two angles are on a straight line with 70°: 180 − 70 = 110°.

mistakes.A: Step 4: 70° is the size of the given pair; the question asks for the OTHER two angles.
mistakes.B: Step 3: x = 30 is not an angle — substitute it into 2x + 10.
mistakes.C: Step 4: the other angles are 180° − 70°, not 180° − 30°. Use the angle, not x.

questions.diagram_alt: Two straight lines crossing; two vertically opposite angles are marked (2x + 10)° and (3x − 20)°, and one of the other angles is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Four angles meet at a point. Two of them are right angles. The other two are equal. How big is each of the other two?
questions.explanation: The two right angles make 180°, leaving 360° − 180° = 180° to share equally: 180° ÷ 2 = 90°. 45° comes from using 180° as the total around a point.
steps: Angles at a point add to 360°.
The two right angles make 90° + 90° = 180°, leaving 360° − 180° = 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 1: angles at a point add to 360°, not 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 180° is shared between TWO equal angles — divide by 2.

questions.prompt: A pie chart has four slices. Three of them have angles 90°, 125° and 80°. What fraction of the whole pie is the fourth slice?
questions.explanation: The fourth slice is 360° − (90° + 125° + 80°) = 65°, and as a fraction of the full 360° that is 65/360 = 13/72. 65/180 wrongly uses 180° as the whole.
steps: Angles at the centre of a pie chart are angles at a point, so they add to 360°.
As a fraction of the whole: 65/360.

mistakes.A: Step 4: 1/4 would be 90° — the fourth slice is 65°, so work out 65/360.
mistakes.B: Step 3: the whole pie is 360°, not 180°.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 1/6 would be 60°; the slice is 65°, so the fraction is 65/360 simplified.
